eastern_catholic.clerical_celibacy.text:
In the Eastern Catholic Churches the ordinary discipline is married clergy: a married man may be ordained deacon and priest, and he continues to live with his wife. A man already ordained may not marry. Bishops are taken from among celibate clergy, usually monks. Celibacy is therefore honored as a monastic and episcopal vocation, not as the only lawful state for a parish priest.

This is the received Eastern discipline, kept when these Churches entered communion with Rome and still named in their particular law. Practice has not been uniform in every country. In some diaspora settings Latin authorities long limited the ordination or assignment of married priests; Eastern Catholics treat those limits as a pastoral restriction on their own rite, not as a change in the rite itself. Unmarried men may still be ordained, and many are. The point Eastern Catholics insist on is that a married parish priesthood is not an exception borrowed from the West, but the Churches' own ancient order.
